questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presented to the hospital with a severe headache for the last week. The patient took no other medications and had no known drug allergies. The patient’s weight and height were 80 kg and 66 inches, respectively. Investigations: Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL ALT 20 units/L CSF microscopy and culture negative CSF cryptococcal antigen positive
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Caspofungin 70 mg IV × one dose, then 50 mg IV once daily
Liposomal amphotericin B 8 mg IV once daily and flucytosine 500 mg by mouth four times daily
Liposomal amphotericin B 350 mg IV once daily and flucytosine 2000 mg by mouth four times daily
Voriconazole 480 mg IV twice daily for 2 doses, then 320 mg IV twice daily.

questions.explanation: Liposomal amphotericin B 350 mg IV once daily and flucytosine 2000 mg by mouth four times daily. The recommended regimen for the treatment of cryptococcal meningitis begins with an induction phase consisting of a combination of liposomal amphotericin B 4 mg/kg per day IV and flucytosine 50–150 mg/kg per day divided into 4 doses and given by mouth every 6 hours for patients with normal renal function. For this patient, correct doses would be liposomal amphotericin B 350 mg and flucytosine 2000 mg by mouth four times daily. Echinocandins like caspofungin have no activity against Cryptococcus. Fluconazole is the recommended medication for the treatment of cryptococcal meningitis during the consolidation and maintenance phases of treatment. It may also be used during the induction phase of therapy but as an alternative to liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine. This patient does not have a contraindication to the use of these agents. Voriconazole is not the recommended medication for the treatment of cryptococcal meningitis but may be considered for salvage therapy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q7

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of fever, headache, and nausea with morning emesis. He was normally well and did not take any regular medications. He lived in California but recently attended a wedding on Vancouver Island, British Columbia. On examination, vital signs were normal. The neck was supple. There was worsening of headache with passively rotating the head from side to side. The remainder of the neurologic examination was unremarkable. Investigations: CT head normal Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 25 cmH2O Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF): Visibly clear on macroscopic appearance CSF protein 50 mg/dL (reference range: 20–40 mg/dL) CSF glucose 50 mg/dL (reference range: 45–80 mg/dL) 300 cells/mm3 (50% lymphocytes, 30% neutrophils) Gram stain:
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cryptococcus gattii Cryptococcus gattii is endemic to parts of British Columbia (including Vancouver Island), the Pacific Northwest, and Australia. The Gram stain in this case demonstrated narrow-based budding yeasts of variable size with thick capsules, suggesting Cryptococcus. Gram stain is not typically the stain of choice – India Ink enables visualization of the capsules. Cryptococcal antigen of CSF has replaced India Ink in many clinical laboratories of the diagnostic of choice for cryptococcal meningitis. The clinical picture and investigations are not suggestive of Candida albicans. Candida spp. can cause meningitis, but it is unusual and typically occurs in medically and surgically compromised patients. The yeasts of C. albicans are 5–8 μm and usually demonstrate pseudohyphae. Cryptococcus neoformans is possible in this case, but it is less likely than C. gattii in an immunocompetent host from an endemic area. C. gattii can be distinguished from C. neoformans by canavanine-glycine-bromthymol blue medium, which turns blue for the former but not the latter. They can also be distinguished by molecular analysis. CNS pneumocystosis is reported, but it is very uncommon and occurs exclusively in immunocompromised hosts. Pneumocystis jirovecii is more commonly associated with pneumonia in immunocompromised patients. The cytopathology is not consistent with P. jirovecii, which does not bud. There is overlap in the cytopathologic and histopathologic appearance of Histoplasma and Cryptococcus spp. They overlap in size, and both demonstrate narrow budding. A thick capsule can be demonstrated for Cryptococcus with mucicarmine stain. Despite its name, H. capsulatum does not have a capsule. However, a thin clearing around the nucleus can appear like a capsule, which resulted in the name. (Image from Murray PR, Rosenthal KS, Pfaller MA. Medical Microbiology. 8th ed. Elsevier; 2016.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q16

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presented with left arm redness accompanied by swelling and pain. The redness had progressed to involve the entire arm and left hand. He had received a number of courses of oral antibiotics with no improvement. He had diabetes mellitus and a living unrelated kidney transplant 15 years earlier for end-stage renal disease. A skin biopsy was performed. Investigations: Skin biopsy: organisms highlighted with Fontana Masson staining
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans The Fontana-Masson stain highlights melanin, which is an important component of cryptococcal cell wall. Cryptococcus neoformans can present atypically in transplant recipients, which leads to delayed diagnosis and treatment. An Alcian Blue stain highlights polysaccharide.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q24

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman from Zimbabwe presented with a 2-week history of increasing confusion, ataxia, headache, and fevers. She was admitted and a lumbar puncture performed after a CT scan of her head. Investigations: HIV-1 Ag/Ab positive CD4 5 cells/μL HIV viral load 225 000 copies/mL Serum CRAG positive CSF: opening pressure 450 mmH2O (120–250) Protein 0.9 g/L (0.15–0.45) Glucose 2.3 mmol/L (plasma glucose 7.2) White blood cells 0.05 ×109/L(50/mm3), 90% lymphocytes Cryptococcal antigen positive CSF cultures: growth on Sab plates consistent with Cryptococcus neoformans She was started on liposomal amphotericin B and 5-flucytosine.
questions.lead_in: When should she be started on antiretrovirals?

options.text: When a repeat CSF is culture negative
When her serum CRAG becomes negative

questions.explanation: After 4 weeks of antifungals Cryptococcosis is one of the few opportunistic infections for which early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (less than 2 weeks) is associated with increased mortality. It is generally recommended to delay ART initiation to at least 4 weeks after start of antifungal therapy to avoid severe immune reconstitution syndrome.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q36

needs: Chapter 128 — Neurologic Diseases and Opportunistic Infections in HIV
questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of fevers, headache, and gradually increasing confusion. The patient was known to have HIV and a history of nonadherence to her antiretroviral therapy. On physical exam, the patient appeared somnolent but had no focal neurologic deficits. A CT head and a lumbar puncture were performed. Investigations: Noncontrasted CT of the head: normal appearances CD4 count 85 cells/μL HIV viral load 450 copies/mL Serum cryptococcal antigen positive 1:128 Lumbar puncture: Opening pressure 32 mmHg CSF WBC count 4/mm3, CSF glucose 30 mg/dL (45–80) CSF total protein 110 mg/dL (20–40) CSF Gram stain negative CSF cryptococcal antigen positive 1:32
questions.lead_in: In addition to starting antifungal therapy, what therapeutic intervention is warranted?
questions.explanation: Serial lumbar punctures The patient has presented with cryptococcal meningitis and evidence of elevated intracranial pressures (ICP). Unlike some other causes of elevation in the ICP , pharmacologic management with either acetazolamide, dexamethasone, or mannitol is not effective in cryptococcal meningitis. The first-line treatment is serial large-volume lumbar punctures to reduce the elevated ICP . Neurosurgical interventions such as lumbar drain placement, ventriculostomy, or VP shunting are reserved for refractory cases or in patients with evidence of imminent herniation.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q23

questions.question: 10.  Cryptococcal meningitis in newly diagnosed HIV from Africa.

parts.text: A.  What is the differential diagnosis for CSF with compatible findings?  Give three things.
B.  She becomes obtunded. Give two urgent steps in management.
C.  What drugs are used for therapy?
D.  When should ART be started? Explain your answer.
E.  What three tests should be done on the CSF?

cohort_answer.text:
Syphilis, toxo, TB
Decrease intracranial pressure with LP/shunt; Manage/protect airway – intubate; Urgent CT to look for herniation
Amphotericin B + flucytosine x 2 weeks then fluconazole 400mg x 8 weeks; Fluconazole 200mg daily until CD4 >100, VL undetectable for >=3mos, at least 12 mos of tx
2-10 weeks after starting treatment to prevent IRIS
Cryptococcal antigen, fungal culture; Opening pressures (if high, do daily LPs do relieve or if requires VPS/EVD)

questions.question: Given india ink+, birdseed+, urease+.

parts.text: What organism?

questions.model_answer: Cryptococcus neoformans (India ink positive encapsulated yeast, brown pigment on birdseed/niger seed agar from melanin production, urease positive).

questions.question: 50+ yo woman, renal transplant for DM nephropathy. 1mo fever, HA, memory loss. CT – no intracranial lesions. LP: opening pressure 50, prot 1.1, glucose 2.1, lymph predominance. Bacterial gram stain was neg, viral PCR neg. Given pic that looks like broad based budding yeast --- but apparently isn’t

parts.text: What is the dx?
How would you manage – treatment and duration (3marks)
What urgent intervention would you do?

questions.model_answer:
a) Diagnosis: cryptococcal meningitis (Cryptococcus neoformans) - narrow-based budding yeast that can be mistaken for the broad-based budding of Blastomyces on cytology/histopathology.
b) Management: induction with liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine for at least 2 weeks, then consolidation with fluconazole 400 mg daily for 8 weeks, followed by maintenance/secondary prophylaxis with fluconazole 200 mg daily for 6-12 months (longer if immunosuppression persists), with attention to reducing immunosuppression as feasible.
c) Urgent intervention: manage the markedly elevated opening pressure (50 cm H2O) with therapeutic large-volume lumbar puncture (repeated serial LPs to reduce pressure to <20 cm H2O or by 50%); a CSF diversion procedure (lumbar drain or ventriculoperitoneal shunt) may be needed if intracranial pressure remains persistently elevated.

questions.question: A 54 year-old, with a history of renal transplant for diabetic nephropathy, presents with subacute confusion and headache. An LP is performed that shows: Opening pressure 50 mmHg, Glucose 2.1, Protein 1.1, Elevated WBC (mostly lymphocytic), Bacterial cultures negative, PCR negative for HSV, VZV. [image-based question: gram stain shown]

parts.text: What is the most likely diagnosis?
Outline the entire treatment course (include names of drugs and durations)
What is one other urgent aspect of therapy?

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Cryptococcal meningitis. Treatment: Induction - liposomal AmB + flucytosine for at least 2 weeks; Consolidation - fluconazole 400-800mg for 8 weeks; Suppression - fluconazole 200-400mg for 6-12 months. Other urgent aspect: reduction of immunosuppressants especially corticosteroid dose, and relieving CSF pressures by LP or other procedures.

questions.question:
Q12 (2006 PM) Cryptococcal meningitis
A 45 year old man with Cryptococcal meningitis

parts.text: What medications are required for a complete course of tx?
B) What sites of infection are there besides the CNS? And what are 2 manifestations in each site?

cohort_answer.text:
Part 1) WHO Guidelines: Initiation - single high dose liposomal ampho B + 14 days flucytosine and fluconazole (COAT trial suggests delaying by 5 weeks vs 1-2 weeks associated with significant reduction in mortality); WHO 2018 guidelines state 4-6 weeks prior to starting HIV treatment. Consolidation - fluconazole 400-800 mg/day for 8-10 weeks. If HIV+: Suppressive - fluconazole 200mg/day for 1-2 years until HIV well controlled and CrAg neg/low (need CD4>100 and VL suppressed for 3 months, minimum 1 year treatment). If non-HIV+: maintenance fluconazole 200mg/d x6-12 months. IDSA 2010: if CSF pressure ≥25 cm CSF and symptoms of increased ICP during induction, relieve by CSF drainage (reduce opening pressure by 50% if extremely high, or to <20 cm CSF) (B-II). Consider discontinuing suppressive therapy during HAART if CD4>100 cells/µL and undetectable/very low HIV RNA sustained ≥3 months (minimum 12 months antifungal therapy) (B-II); reinstitute if CD4 decreases <100 (B-III). For asymptomatic antigenemia: perform LP and blood culture; if positive treat as symptomatic meningoencephalitis/disseminated disease; without evidence of meningoencephalitis treat with fluconazole 400mg/day orally until immune reconstitution.

Part B) Lungs: nodules, lobar infiltrates, interstitial infiltrates, cavities, endobronchial masses/colonization, ARDS, mediastinal/hilar adenopathy, PTX, pleural effusions/empyema, miliary pattern. Skin: papules/maculopapules, subcutaneous abscess, vesicle, plaque, cellulitis, purpura, acne, draining sinus, ulcer, bullae. Bone/Joints: osteolytic lesion, arthritis, myositis. Heart/blood vessels: cryptococcemia, endocarditis, mycotic aneurysm, myocarditis, pericarditis, infected vascular graft. GI tract: nodular/ulcerative lesions, esophageal nodule, peritonitis, pancreatic mass. Breast: abscess, LAD. Thyroid: thyroiditis, mass. Adrenal: insufficiency, mass. Eye: papilledema, extraocular muscle paresis, keratitis, chorioretinitis, endophthalmitis, optic nerve atrophy.

parts.text: What drugs are used for tx?

cohort_answer.text: Induction: Amphotericin B 3-5 mg/kg/d + Flucytosine 100mg/kg/d in 4 divided doses for 2 weeks. Consolidation: Fluconazole 400mg/day x min 8 weeks. Maintenance: Fluconazole 200mg daily for more than a year until CD4>100. New WHO guidelines: amphoB 10mg/kg IV x1 with 2 weeks fluc + flucytosine in HIV+ patients with crypto meningitis, consolidation and maintenance same

parts.text: When should ART be started? Explain your answer

cohort_answer.text: Earlier ART can be detrimental in CNS infections. Delay ARV by at least 5 weeks per COAT trial to reduce risk of cryptococcal IRIS. Low CSF WBC count at diagnosis associated with greatest risk of IRIS with ART initiation

cohort_answer.text: CrAg; Cell count + diff, glucose, protein; Gram stain, india ink stain, culture

questions.question: Allogeneic bone marrow transplant recently treated for bacterial pneumonia. Recently travelled for several months through the United States. Now presenting with meningitis. CSF is sent to the lab for testing.

parts.text: What are 2 reasons for the scenario: Positive India Ink / Negative cryptococcal antigen test
What are 2 reasons for the scenario: Negative India Ink / Positive cryptococcal antigen test
What antifungal should you not use and give 2 reasons why.
In 5 days, the lab is growing a white mycelia on culture. 2 possibilities?

questions.model_answer:
a) Positive India ink / negative cryptococcal antigen: (1) false-positive India ink (misinterpretation of artifact, lymphocytes, or another encapsulated/budding yeast as Cryptococcus) (2) prozone effect with a very high antigen titer causing a false-negative result on latex agglutination-based CrAg testing (less of an issue with the newer lateral flow assay).
b) Negative India ink / positive cryptococcal antigen: (1) low fungal burden below the detection threshold of microscopy (India ink is insensitive, particularly in non-HIV hosts, roughly 50% sensitive) while CrAg detects capsular antigen at much lower organism burden (2) inexperienced reader/technical/sampling issue missing the organism on direct microscopy.
c) Antifungal to avoid: conventional (deoxycholate) amphotericin B - reasons: (1) significant nephrotoxicity, compounded by concurrent nephrotoxic immunosuppressants (e.g., calcineurin inhibitors) in a transplant recipient (2) infusion-related reactions and electrolyte wasting (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia); a lipid formulation (liposomal amphotericin B) should be used instead.
d) White mycelial growth at 5 days: two possibilities are a dimorphic endemic fungus in its mold phase acquired during US travel - Histoplasma capsulatum or Blastomyces dermatitidis (Coccidioides immitis is another possibility in the correct geographic exposure).
